sources.entry: AF_XDP - Defines the socket and UMEM rings handing XDP frames to user space, and the zero-copy and need-wakeup modes.

summary.title: AF_XDP
summary.one_liner: Learn how AF_XDP sockets move packets from an XDP program into user space using UMEM memory and FILL, COMPLETION, RX and TX rings, plus the zero-copy, copy and need-wakeup modes.
takeaways: AF_XDP sockets receive and send frames via RX and TX rings that point into a shared UMEM memory region, with FILL and COMPLETION rings transferring frame ownership between kernel and user space.
An XDP program redirects packets to a socket through an XSKMAP using bpf_redirect_map(); packets are dropped if the map entry is empty or the socket does not match the device and queue.
XDP_ZEROCOPY and XDP_COPY bind flags force a mode, and XDP_USE_NEED_WAKEUP reduces syscalls by signalling when poll() or sendto() is needed.
Multi-buffer support (XDP_USE_SG, XDP_PKT_CONTD) lets a packet span several frames in both copy and zero-copy modes.
summary.summary: This is the Linux kernel documentation page for AF_XDP, an address family for high-performance packet processing. It explains the socket setup: the UMEM registration, the four rings (FILL, COMPLETION, RX, TX), binding to a device and queue, and the XSKMAP used by the XDP program to redirect frames. It then documents configuration flags and socket options such as XDP_COPY, XDP_ZEROCOPY, need_wakeup, XDP_SHARED_UMEM, and XDP_STATISTICS, followed by multi-buffer support with pseudo-code for RX and TX paths. The reader is assumed to know BPF and XDP already.
